correctness.rationale: Two independent generators agree on all 2,927 faces. Two lexicographically opposite exhaustive acyclic matchings were checked over 11,844 incidences. Exact augmented integral Morse boundaries have, respectively, rank-eleven unit Smith differential and ranks one and eighteen with unit Smith factors. The explicit 11-by-11 determinant-one minor, independent mod-two ranks and exact signed \(C_7\)-orbit chain ranks substantiate reduced integral homology and rational character; verified standalone code outputs recorded.

originality.rationale: The two founding multipath-complex papers define path-poset topology and give transitive-tournament results, but these do not determine the regular directed-cycle tournament on Z/7 nor its exact integral homology or nontrivial cyclic character. Inspected quiver-minor blow-up results require directed acyclicity for their matching-complex equivalence; bidirected polygons and directed flag/tournaplex constructions are different. Queries over cyclic/regular/consecutive-difference tournaments and exact rank parameters, together with the accessible previous claims and available published research records, disclosed no covering result. This is a best-knowledge comparison, not a proof of uniqueness.
residual_risks: No search certifies a negative; a specialized unindexed tournament calculation could reproduce some ranks or the cyclic character.
The topological homotopy type and nontrivial higher attaching maps remain undetermined; the theorem deliberately asserts only homology and rational symmetry.

value.rationale: The canonical regular consecutive-difference tournament is naturally motivated as a cyclic, nontransitive counterpart to the classified transitive-tournament multipath complexes. The precise nontrivial three-degree integral homology and different rational fixed/cyclotomic summands answer motivated invariants; they are not inferred from Euler characteristic or generic homotopy results. The theorem offers a reproducible benchmark without pretending to give a general family or homotopy decomposition.
